title: If This, Then That
tagline: Your program starts making decisions instead of just following orders.
builtOn: Lesson 5 — your world full of objects.
goals: Use an `if` statement to make your program choose what to do
Declare variables that track information over time, like `int score`
Show text and numbers on screen with `text()`
Explain that a program can be in different **states** — playing, game over

vocab.def: "if this is true, do this block of code"
a value that is only ever `true` or `false`. Nothing in between
a named container for a value. `int score = 0;` names a box called score that starts at zero
a variable that holds a whole number — 0, 7, -3. No decimals
a Processing function that draws words or numbers on the screen
which mode your program is in right now — playing, or game over, or paused

warmup: How did you add 12 coins to your world last time? Which loop did you use, and where did it go?

howItWorks.h: Variables that live at the top
p: Up until now your variables have been things you created and used. Now you need variables that **remember** something across frames — like a score that keeps going up.
Those go at the very **top** of your sketch, outside `setup()` and outside `draw()`.

code.label: Global variables

bullets: Written up there, **every** function can see them.
Written inside `setup()`, they vanish the second `setup()` finishes and `draw()` cannot see them at all.

p: An `if` asks a yes-or-no question. If the answer is yes, the code inside the braces runs. If not, it is skipped entirely.

code.label: A question and an answer

bullets: The thing in the parentheses is a **condition** — it is either true or false.
`>` greater than, `<` less than, `>=` at least, `<=` at most, `==` exactly equal.
Careful: `==` is a question ("are these equal?"). A single `=` is a command ("make this equal to that"). Mixing them up is a classic.

p: A `boolean` is the simplest possible variable: it is `true` or it is `false`.
`!` means **NOT**. So `!gameOver` reads as "not game over" — in other words, "the game is still going."

code.label: Two states, one choice

p: `text()` draws words. You give it what to say and where to put it.

code.label: Showing the score
code.body:
fill(50);                          // the text color
textSize(24);                      // how big
text("Score: " + score, 20, 36);   // what, then x, then y

bullets: The `+` glues the words `"Score: "` and the number `score` together into one piece of text.
Set `fill()` **before** `text()`, or your text takes whatever color the last shape used.

p: This is the big idea. Your game is not one thing — it is in a **mode**. Right now there are two: playing, and game over.
The `boolean gameOver` remembers which mode you are in, and the `if/else` in `draw()` picks which one to run. Everything else follows from that.

steps: At the **very top**, above `setup()`, add: `int score = 0;` and `boolean gameOver = false;`
In `draw()`, after `background()`, add a `text()` call showing the score. Run it. You should see `Score: 0` in the corner.
Test it: temporarily change `int score = 0;` to `int score = 7;` and run. The display should change. Set it back to 0.
Now move all your game code out of `draw()` and into a new function called `playGame()`. Look at the starter code to see exactly how.
In `draw()`, add the `if (!gameOver) { playGame(); } else { showGameOver(); }` block.
Write the `showGameOver()` function. Run it — it should still play normally, since `gameOver` is false.
Test the other branch: temporarily change `boolean gameOver = false;` to `true` and run. You should jump straight to the game over screen. Set it back.
Add the trigger: inside `playGame()`, `if (score >= 10) { gameOver = true; }`
Change what triggers game over, and restyle the game over screen so it sounds like your game.

code.label: Main sketch tab

makeItYours: Change what triggers game over. A time limit? A score above 20? Something else entirely?
Restyle the game over screen — different words, different colors, a message that fits your game.
Add a second variable: a `lives` counter that starts at 3 and counts down.
Make the background color change as the score goes up — a few `if` statements stacked up.
Show more than the score. A timer, a level number, a message that appears at a milestone.
challenge: Make the game react in layers — the background shifts at score 5, the text turns red at score 8, and lives count down at the same time. Multiple variables and multiple conditions working together.
flintHint: Good things to ask: "my score will not show up on screen", "what is the difference between = and ==?", or "how do I make my background change when the score goes up?" Paste your `playGame()` in if something will not run.
wrapup: What is the difference between an `int` and a `boolean`? Give an example of each from your own game.
assignmentTask: Give your game a memory and a mind. It should track something, show it, and change what it does based on it.
assignmentDo: Declare at least one variable at the top of your sketch that changes over time.
Use an `if` to branch the game into two different states — playing and game over.
Make the trigger and the game over screen **yours**. Do not leave the starter's "You Win!" if that is not what your game is about.
submit: Two screenshots: one of the game playing, one of your game over screen.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Declare a variable and change it over time.
Write an `if` statement that branches behavior.
Show a value on screen with `text()`.
Explain what a `boolean` is and give an example.
standard: Use `if`, changing variables (`int score`), and `text()` to make the program react and track state.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: My score or text will not show, or my `if` never triggers. **Next step:** declare your variables at the **top** (outside `setup` and `draw`) so every function can see them, and double-check your `if` condition.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: A variable changes during play, shows on screen with `text()`, and an `if` branches the game (playing vs. game over).

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I changed what triggers the state change (a time limit, a different score), restyled the game-over screen, or added a second variable like `lives`.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I combined multiple conditions or variables so the game reacts in layered ways — the background shifts as score rises, lives count down, and so on.

thinking: In one or two sentences: what state does your game track, and what flips it from one state to another?

di.h: Global scope — say why, not just where
p: `int score = 0;` and `boolean gameOver = false;` go above `setup()`. "These live outside `setup()` and `draw()` so all functions can see them."
Students will try to declare them inside `setup()`. When they do, the variable disappears the instant `setup()` ends. Show that failure once if you have time — the error message is not obvious.
"The condition in the parentheses is either true or false. The code inside the braces runs only when it is true."
Demo something loud and visible: `if (score > 10) { background(255, 0, 0); }` and then set the score by hand to show both branches.
Worth thirty explicit seconds. A single `=` **assigns**; a double `==` **asks**. Write both on the board.
In Java the compiler will usually catch `if (score = 10)`, which is a mercy, but they need the vocabulary to read the error.
`fill(0); textSize(24); text("Score: " + score, 20, 36);`
"The `+` here glues text and a number together into one string." Do not use the word *concatenation*.
Point out that `fill()` has to come **before** `text()`, or the text inherits whatever color the last shape used. This will bite someone.
`if (!gameOver) { ...play... } else { ...show game over... }`
"`!` means NOT — so `if not gameOver` means `if the game is still going`."
This is the structural idea of the lesson. The game has **modes**, a variable remembers which one, and `draw()` picks. Everything in Lessons 7 and 9 builds on this shape.

di.h: Build it up in stages, not all at once
p: Variable declared → changed in `draw()` → displayed on screen → used in an `if` to branch. Four separate runs.
Pasting the whole finished structure at once hides where each piece came from.

guided: Add the two global variables at the top together. Run — nothing changes yet.
Add the `text()` call so the score shows. Run. Now there is something on screen to react to.
**Test by cheating:** change `int score = 0;` to `int score = 7;` and run. The display updates. Set it back. Testing a display by hand-setting the value is a real technique and worth naming.
Refactor together: move the game body from `draw()` into `playGame()`. Run — nothing should change. Emphasise that: a refactor that changes nothing visible is a *success*.
Add the `if/else` in `draw()` and write `showGameOver()`. Run — still plays normally.
**Test the other branch by cheating:** set `gameOver = true` in the declaration and run. Straight to the game over screen. Set it back.
Add the real trigger (`if (score >= 10)`). Release for personalization.
pitfalls: **Declaring globals inside `setup()`.** Scope error. The most common structural mistake in this lesson.
**`fill()` after `text()`** — text comes out in an unexpected color.

**`textAlign(CENTER, CENTER)` never reset.** It affects every later `text()` call, so the score display in the corner silently moves. The starter resets it with `textAlign(LEFT, TOP)` at the end of `showGameOver()` — make sure students who restyle that function keep the reset.

Nothing ever changes `score`, so the `if` can never fire. Note out loud that coins are drawn but **not yet collectable** — that is Lesson 7. Some students will find this unsatisfying; tell them the payoff is next lesson.
Forgetting the braces on a one-line `if` and then adding a second line later that runs unconditionally.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: `int` holds a whole number (score, lives, level). `boolean` holds only true or false (gameOver, paused). Look for an example from their own sketch, not a generic one.
notes: `score++` is shorthand for `score = score + 1`. Fine to mention if a student asks, but keep `score = score + 1` in the starter so the operation stays explicit.
Coins are drawn but not collected yet. Say this up front so students do not spend the period hunting for a bug that is not there.
The "test by cheating" move — hand-setting a variable to check a branch — is a genuine debugging skill. Name it while you use it.
Only **one** new concept today: `if`. Variables and `text()` are the supporting cast. If a student is struggling, drop the `playGame()` refactor and just get an `if` working in `draw()`.
Fast finishers: layered conditions, or a `lives` counter. Both are extensions of the same idea rather than new ones.
